new_statements.quote: p.160: "Although tonal contrast is found in virtually all of the the Lakes Plain languages, it will not be shown in the word list transcriptions. Additionally, stress is not marked because only a few original word lists marked it and it has not been found to be contrastive in any of the Lakes Plain languages to date." p.152: "Tone is a prominent feature of all Lakes Plain languages and therefore was most likely a feature of some of the protolanguages as well. [...] All the modern languages have at least high and low tone. [...] Obokuitai has a fall (Jenison 1991), Doutai (McAllister 1991), Edopi (Kim 1995) and all the western Tariku languages have a fall and a rise (Clouse n.d.1)."

new_statements.rule_in_words: Kirikiri (a western Tariku / Lakes Plain language) is tonal, with high, low, falling and rising tones (Clouse 2002 counts six phonemic tone patterns); stress has not been found to be contrastive in any Lakes Plain language, and no source states a position for word stress.
new_statements.exceptions: None; the stress remark is a blanket statement about the Lakes Plain family based on the author's own Kirikiri fieldwork (1989-1992) and the other SIL phonologies; the tone remark cites Heljä Clouse's unpublished 'An autosegmental approach to Kirikiri tone (notes)'.
new_statements.domain_note: Comparative 267-item word lists (citation forms); statement is family-level (all Lakes Plain languages), not a Kirikiri-specific phonology section.
new_statements.identity_note: Clouse 1997's stress remark is family-level ("any of the Lakes Plain languages") but comes from the Kirikiri fieldworker (D. & H. Clouse, Wahuka, 1989-1992), and the tone remark applies to Kirikiri as a western Tariku language (via Heljä Clouse's unpublished Kirikiri tone notes). Kirikiri has three dialect groups Kirikiri, Taû and Faia (Glottolog: Nuclear Kirikiri nucl1599, Faia faia1238; Faia 89% cognate per Clouse 1997: 148); the Clouse data are from the Kirikiri (Wahuka) dialect.

sources.citation: Clouse, Duane A. 2002. Kirikiri. In Melvin Ember, Carol R. Ember and Ian Skoggard (eds.), Encyclopedia of World Cultures Supplement, 168-171. New York: Macmillan Reference. (full text at https://www.encyclopedia.com/humanities/encyclopedias-almanacs-transcripts-and-maps/kirikiri)
sources.note: Linguistic Affiliation paragraph only: 'Kirikiri is an isolating and tonal language with six phonemic consonants (f,b,t,l,s,k), seven phonemic vowels (i,I,e,a,o,u,U, where I and U are fricated variants of the high vowels) and six phonemic tone patterns.' Nothing on stress.

sources.citation: Clouse, Helja and Duane Clouse. 1993. Kirikiri and the Western Lakes Plains languages: selected phonological phenomena. Language and Linguistics in Melanesia 24(1): 1-18. (image-only scan from https://www.langlxmelanesia.com/llm-archive, Vol. 24 No. 1)
sources.note: Kirikiri-centred segmental study (consonant lenition, nasals, seven-vowel system with fricativised vowels incl. spectrographic data from 8 Kirikiri speakers, diphthongs, semivowels). Silent on stress; tone only in fn.7 and conclusion p.16: 'Further research on these languages in the areas of syllable structure and tone will, hopefully, shed more light'.
